entries.title: After clinching playoff berth, White Sox want 'to do everything in our power to win this division'
entries.summary: <p>Clinching a playoff spot Thursday in Kansas City was a <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/09/24/white-sox-players-always-believed-their-stunning-playoff-berth-was-possible-sean-burke-chris-getz-will-venable-davis-martin-colson-montgomery-miguel-vargas" target="_blank" ><u>a moment of tremendous catharsis</u></a> for a <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox" target="_blank" >White Sox</a> team that had worked to defy expectations all season — and especially for those who had labored to pull the franchise out of the morass that was the 121-loss season in 2024.</p><p>‘‘Me, [Miguel] Vargas, [Andrew Benintendi], Davis [Martin] have been here since ‘24,’’ right-hander Sean Burke said in a beer- and champagne-soaked visitors’ clubhouse in Kauffman Stadium. ‘‘To see the journey it took to get back to this spot is super-rewarding.’’</p><p>But the celebration couldn’t go on forever. <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/09/24/white-sox-prioritizing-rest-division-race-as-they-set-final-rotation-order-will-venable-sean-burke-davis-martin-anthony-kay-david-sandlin-luis-castillo-tyler-davis" target="_blank" ><u>Burke was the scheduled starter Friday</u></a> against the Rockies in what possibly was his most important outing to date.</p><p>The Sox entered their final series of the regular season one game behind the Guardians in the American League Central with three games to play. But they own the season-series tiebreaker, which means finishing in a tie with the Guardians would give them the division.</p><p>‘‘The work is not done,’’ general manager Chris Getz said. ‘‘We’re certainly going to do everything in our power to win this division. We know the significance of that.’’</p><p>The significance of a division title is easy enough to measure through Burke, the Sox’ most reliable starter (3.40 ERA in 167 innings pitched entering Friday). If the Sox catch the Guardians, they likely will secure a bye through the wild-card round and not play until next Saturday. That could set up Burke as their Game 1 starter.</p><p>If not, the Sox must begin a wild-card series Tuesday after deploying Burke, Martin and Anthony Kay — their three leaders in innings pitched this season — this weekend.</p><p>A lot might be asked of Kay, in particular. With left-handed relievers Hagen Smith and Sean Newcomb each working two innings Wednesday, Kay was available out of the bullpen Friday for roughly 20 pitches, even though he remains the scheduled starter Sunday.</p><p>It’s a cost that’s easier to pay if it provides the benefit of six days off — and one that might prove prohibitive if it affects the results of a best-of-three series next week instead.</p><p>‘‘That’s what ‘all hands on deck’ mentality is all about,’’ manager Will Venable said. ‘‘We want to win the division. To do that, we need to put together three really good games, so we don’t feel we are in a [bad] spot to set things up for down the road.’’</p><p>For as much as the Sox celebrated clinching a playoff berth as the historic moment in MLB history it was, there is a decided ‘‘division or bust’’ nature to their strategy for the final weekend.</p><p>‘‘It’s pretty straightforward,’’ Venable said. ‘‘You’ve gotta push. I don’t think there’s any other choice. I don’t know why you wouldn’t.’’</p><p>At the same time, Getz agreed with a reporter’s premise that the Sox’ front office had enjoyed a sort of win-win with their trade-deadline approach. Getz declined to deal any of the Sox’ best prospects, and the team still made the playoffs.</p><p>‘‘We feel like we’re still just getting started,’’ Getz said, pointing to a stable of players with years of team control left. ‘‘We certainly didn’t want to mortgage the future.’’</p><p>But that’s a big-picture, long-term view that begins and ends with the front office. For the Sox’ clubhouse, every day from here on out will be spent living in the moment. That means showering each other in beer on Thursday in Kansas City and fighting for an AL Central title for the rest of the weekend.</p><p>‘‘You clinch a playoff spot [Thursday] but have so much on the line here this weekend,’’ Venable said. ‘‘Ultimately, these guys understand where we are at, how important these games are and what it means to go out there and continue to be locked in and play the kind of baseball we’ve been playing.’’</p>

entries.title: Fans are feeling South Side pride for postseason-bound White Sox
entries.summary: <p>Angelica Flores didn’t grow up watching sports, but at Friday’s game against the Colorado Rockies, she wholeheartedly embraced the Sox fandom.</p><p>The game was at least her eighth this season, she said.</p><p>“But we watch every night,” said her boyfriend, Miguel Ortega. “Every game. Sometimes wear Pope hats too to bring them good luck.”</p><p>The DeKalb couple has been together for five years. That was her first introduction to the team she now dons black and white for religiously.</p><p>Ortega, 30, has been going to Sox games for decades and grew up loving the team.</p><p>The couple was among many fans at Rate Field who have caught postseason fever after the Sox clinched a postseason berth for the first time since 2021. </p><p>For Will Barbee, 53, Friday was an opportunity to share the winning spirit with his 14 children.</p><p>Barbee and his kids, who ranged in age from 6 to 23, don’t often get to attend a game all together. So it was made even sweeter that this one comes 24 hours after the team qualified for playoff baseball.</p><p>“The crowd speaks for itself,” Barbee said. “When you're good, people watch you. entries.title: White Sox shortstop Colson Montgomery sets new MLB single-season record for strikeouts
entries.summary: <p>With a full-count take on a 93 mph Tomoyuki Sugano fastball down the middle, White Sox shortstop <b>Colson Montgomery</b> set a new MLB single-season record for strikeouts with 224 on Friday night, passing the record <b>Mark Reynolds</b> set in 2009.</p><p>A long-levered power hitter, strikeouts have been and will be part of Montgomery’s game. The larger problem is his overall fall-off in production. Montgomery has 31 home runs and 87 RBI while playing solid defense at shortstop, but entered Friday with a .615 OPS and a 39% strikeout rate since June 1.</p><p>“Strikeouts have created some frustration for him,” said general manager <b>Chris Getz.</b> “But he can still help. He's been very consistent on the defensive side. Obviously he's come through with some big hits and some big home runs. But he's still continuing to grow.”</p><p>While Sox leadership has backed Montgomery, he’s gone from a middle of the lineup mainstay to batting eighth on Friday night. If there’s a solace for the 24-year-old’s new place in history, it’s that individual numbers feel a lot less relevant after the Sox clinched a playoff spot on Thursday.</p><p>“Ws are all that matters,” Montgomery said on Thursday. “Whatever I can do to help the team, that's all I care about. Anything else, especially right now, I don't give a [expletive] about it."</p><p><b>Meidroth dealing with sore hamstring</b></p><p>His sore left wrist is public knowledge, but White Sox second baseman <b>Chase Meidroth</b> is <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/09/22/chase-meidroth-brings-fire-to-surprising-white-sox-team-colson-montgomery-kyle-teel-randal-grichuk-chris-getz-mike-vasil-derek-shomon-ryan-fuller-justin-jirschele" target="_blank" ><u>known for playing through so many maladies</u></a> that <b>Will Venable</b> had to specify what prompted his early exit on Thursday.</p><p>“Sore left hamstring,” Venable said. “Him against the [left-handed starters Saturday and Sunday] is really important. Wanted to give him a little bit of a blow [Friday]. He’ll be available off the bench.”</p><p>Only <b>Miguel Vargas</b> has more plate appearances or produced–per wins above replacement (WAR)--more value on the Sox this year than Meidroth. To Venable’s point, Meidroth has hit .346/.428/.583 against left-handers this season. If his hamstring only allows him to play two games this weekend, matchups against Rockies southpaws <b>Jose Quintana</b> and <b>Kyle Freeland</b> on Saturday and Sunday are worth prioritizing.</p><p><b>Brazoban back in form?</b></p><p>Just when it seemed the White Sox were getting nothing from trade deadline acquisitions, <b>Brenton Doyle</b> entered Friday with an .800 OPS in September, and <b>Huascar Brazoban </b>has returned from the injured list with three consecutive scoreless appearances.</p><p>Acquired from the Mets for two prospects, the 36-year-old right-hander yielded runs in five of his last six appearances before being sidelined with a left lat strain in late-August. It might sound weird for a right-handed pitcher to miss time for an injury to his left arm, but Brazoban’s command struggles were the result of trying to pitch through it.</p><p>“The left arm is important for me too, because it’s how you point where your pitches are going,” Brazoban told the Sun-Times via interpreter. “I tried to fight through that, but I reached a point where I couldn’t. I was wasting opportunities for my team, and I didn’t want to do that.”</p><p>Now healthy, the nasty changeup the Sox acquired Brazoban for is back on display, as he struck out a pair of hitters with it in a scoreless inning of work on Thursday.</p><p>“Every one of us that is in the major leagues has a little magic,” Brazoban said via interpreter. “Mine is that.”<br></p>

entries.title: Swept by Red Sox in weather-forced doubleheader, Cubs face pitching questions on eve of playoffs
entries.summary: <p>BOSTON – It’s the eve of the postseason, and the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs" >Cubs</a> have some questions to answer.</p><p>Most pressingly, it’s who they’re going to face in an opening-round series and where that best-of-three series will be played.</p><p>They were swept by the Red Sox in Friday’s doubleheader, widening the gap between them and the first-place Padres in the NL wild-card standings.</p><p>But there are questions on the pitching front, too.</p><p>Righty <b>Clay Holmes</b> has not been the dominant arm he was when he joined the Cubs in a deadline deal. After allowing just a single run in four consecutive August starts, he’s had a bumpy September, with an 8.24 ERA and 15 walks in his last four trips to the mound.</p><p>That includes the three runs he allowed in Game 1’s 4-3 loss Friday. But the walks are the most glaring issue as the Cubs approach the playoffs.</p><p>“The big thing is really allowing the defense to work,” Holmes said. “It comes down to filling the zone up, and when I do that, good things happen. The pitch count stays down, and I rely on my strengths.</p><p>“Really, it’s just filling the zone up more, and it’ll put us in a much better place.”</p><p>Lefty <b>David Peterson</b> once seemed like the odd starter out of a playoff rotation, but he’s been one of their hottest hands down the stretch. He tossed five shutout innings in Game 2 – a 2-0 Cubs loss – on Friday and has a 1.27 ERA in his last four outings.</p><p>“This is the time of year when you’ve got to be at your best,” Peterson said. “As you come down the stretch as a starter, you don’t necessarily know if you’re going to be starting or coming out of the bullpen in the playoffs. It’s trying to get your stuff as sharp as possible and be at your best going into it.”</p><p>Throw in the uncertainty surrounding righty <b>Kevin Gausman</b> and his banged-up shoulder, and there’s a lot of mystery right now when it comes to what next week looks like for the Cubs.</p><p>That includes where they’ll play, who they’ll play and which pitchers they’ll throw.</p><p>“For us, it’s to be able to make the decision for them as hard as possible,” Peterson said of the starting group. “Every guy has raised the bar and gotten ready for what’s next. It’s a good problem to have to make tough decisions.”</p><p><b>From Fenway to Florida</b></p><p>After playing a weather-impacted doubleheader Friday, the team’s final game before the postseason was <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/09/25/cubs-red-sox-game-moved-boston-weather-fenway-park-tampa-bay-florida-tropicana-field" >forced to Florida</a> by severe weather coming to Boston.</p><p>The Cubs and Red Sox will finish their series Sunday afternoon at Tropicana Field, home of the Rays, in St. Petersburg, Florida. That game starts at 2:05 p.m. Central.</p><p>A scene change might be good news for a struggling Cubs lineup to get out of the wind and cold.</p><p>“We have all the confidence in the world in this group,” left fielder <b>Ian Happ</b> said. “And we get to play in a dome on Sunday, some neutral conditions. It will be good for some guys to get some knocks and carry some momentum [into the playoffs].”</p><p><b>Bullpen move</b></p><p>The Cubs placed right-hander <b>Edward Cabrera</b> on the Family Medical Emergency List on Friday, filling his place in the bullpen by bringing righty <b>Gavin Hollowell</b> off the injured list.</p><p>Cabrera struggled last time out, allowing three runs on two hits, two walks and a hit batter while recording only two outs against the Marlins.</p><p>Hollowell got into Game 2 on Friday but hadn’t pitched since the end of August. He entered Friday with a 2.51 ERA in 14 appearances this season.</p>

entries.title: Alex Bregman returns to Cubs’ lineup, which needs to get back to ‘crushing it’ to win in playoffs
entries.summary: <p>BOSTON – Just five days after getting <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/09/23/cubs-alex-bregman-face-injury-return-matt-shaw-bunt-daniel-palencia-stats" >hit in the face with a foul ball</a> and suffering multiple facial fractures, Alex Bregman was back in action.</p><p>The third baseman served as the designated hitter in the first game of the team’s doubleheader Friday, and while he didn’t get on base – going 0-for-4 and striking out with two runners in scoring position – his presence meant plenty for the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs" >Cubs</a>.</p><p>Not that his teammates needed a reminder of <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/08/07/cubs-alex-bregman-home-run-ryan-zeferjahn-bullpen-pitcher-mlb-trade-deadline-angels" >what kind of player Bregman is</a>, but they got one anyway, witnessing firsthand what it took to come back from such a scary moment in a matter of days.</p><p>“Breggy, everybody knows the competitor he is and how much he puts into this game. But to see him tackle this adversity head on, his mentality never waivered,” starting pitcher Clay Holmes said. “He never showed any signs of being defeated. There was no question in his mind he was going to be back.”</p><p>Of course, there’s the baseball aspect of Bregman’s presence, too, and having the team’s second best hitter ready to go for the postseason – which begins Tuesday – is a huge deal for the Cubs as they look to make a run deep into October.</p><p>“I’m excited for the postseason. I’m looking forward to it,” Bregman said. “[Friday] was, ‘Let’s get some at-bats and get back to getting in the swing of things.’</p><p>“I wanted to make sure that I wasn’t thinking anything about my face and the only thing I was thinking about was how I normally think when I’m playing the game of baseball. And that was good. I didn’t think about it one time. All I was thinking about was what I normally go through in the batter’s box and in the dugout.</p><p>“The mechanics were terrible today. Hopefully, I’ll fix those and get back to crushing it.”</p><p>That’s the Cubs’ hope, too, and after watching this team the last four days, it could really use someone to start crushing it.</p><p>The Cubs – who woke up Friday as baseball’s highest scoring team and second in the sport in home runs – scored a total of nine runs and hit one homer in their last five games. That included two runs in each of their three contests against the Marlins earlier this week, three runs in Game 1 of Friday’s doubleheader and zero in Game 2. The only homer came off Seiya Suzuki’s bat in Thursday’s <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/09/24/cubs-clinch-mlb-postseason-playoffs-pete-crow-armstrong-matthew-boyd-nl-wild-card-standings-red-sox-doubleheader" >playoff-clinching victory</a>.</p><p>Perhaps it’s not surprising they went 1-4.</p><p>Sure, the conditions helped. It was a cool, windy three days at Wrigley Field, and <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/09/25/cubs-red-sox-game-moved-boston-weather-fenway-park-tampa-bay-florida-tropicana-field" >the storms coming to Boston</a> meant more wind Friday at Fenway Park. At least two balls the Cubs hit would have been home runs in normal conditions, maybe a third, which obviously impacted the outcome.</p><p>“We hit three homers [in Game 1] that didn’t go out of the park. That’s offense,” manager Craig Counsell said. “We should have had six runs on the board. We had three. That’s how I saw it.”</p><p>But whether it’s stiff wind or stiff competition, the postseason will bring more challenges to the Cubs’ offense.</p><p>Bregman’s presence ought to help. But there will need to be contributions from all over the place to get the Cubs scoring runs in a way that will win playoff games.</p><p>“We haven’t swung it as well the last few days. But it takes one swing, honestly, for the whole lineup,” Bregman said. “This time of year, you’ve got to turn the page quickly. I know everyone wants to [say], ‘Oh, they haven’t hit for three days.’ But you’ve got to turn the page quickly and move onto the next pitch.</p><p>“There’s going to be games in the playoffs where we need to win games where we score three runs. And there’s going to be games where we can score a lot of runs and the offense will be rolling. We’ve got to figure out a way to do a little bit better than we’ve done the last few days.</p><p>“But it comes down to the next pitch, and that’s it. That’s the mentality in there.”</p>

entries.title: Welch urged to do more than apologize for Benton harassment case
entries.summary: <p>Last month, House Speaker Emanuel “Chris” Welch told WGN Political Editor Tahman Bradley during an interview, “I'm going to apologize for making her feel uncomfortable.”</p><p>The woman he was referring to was a district office worker for former Rep. Harry Benton, D-Plainfield, who who quit after she said she was sexually harassed. The woman also told the Chicago Tribune that Welch had sent “heart-eye” emojis to her mobile phone in response to photos and said when she reached out to Welch about her future career plans, he suggested that they meet at a bar in his favorite suburban steakhouse. All of that, she said made her feel quite uncomfortable.</p><p>“I'm going to own that. I regret it, and I want to apologize to her,” Welch told Bradley. “I sincerely want to apologize to her because it was never my intent to make her or anyone feel uncomfortable.”</p><p>So, I reached out to the young former staffer through an approved intermediary to ask if Welch had ever apologized to her.</p><p>“No, he’s never apologized to me,” she replied.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-floatRight><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-960000" name="module-960000"></a> <div class="RichTextSidebarModule-title">Columnist </div> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h2>Columnists</h2></div> </div><p>When I asked whether she thinks Welch “should” apologize, the former staffer said there was something else he should do along with an apology: “I think I'd like to hear how he plans to improve the culture along with the apology,” she said. “Empty apology for his actions alone would just be awkward,” she continued.</p><p>I showed the back-and-forth between me and the intermediary to several House Democrats. Most said the culture change was more important.</p><p>Rep. Kelly Cassidy, D-Chicago, who has been a Welch critic, had this to say: “I agree with her perspective. A personal apology is empty unless backed with significant action. We need to fix the policies and procedures that failed her, but also the culture that led to the harm in the first place.”</p><p>Cassidy also didn’t expect that a Welch-style apology would be sufficient: “I have issues with apologies that focus on the feelings of the victim as opposed to his actions.”</p><p>“I've always been less interested in apologies and more concerned with fixing problems,” said Rep. Mary Beth Canty, D-Arlington Heights, who also chairs the House Women’s Caucus.</p><p>“I think her comment that she’d like substantive cultural changes and not just an apology makes sense and is wise,” said Rep. Anna Moeller, D-Elgin. “From what I’ve heard, the working group assembled by the speaker is taking the task seriously, and I think the caucus will be looking for substantive proposals to help ensure that district staff are protected. I think if the speaker knew that she’d like a direct apology he would provide one.”</p><p>Well, he knows now.</p><p>Rep. Will Guzzardi, D-Chicago, is a member of Welch’s leadership team: “All of us, especially those of us in leadership, bear responsibility for the workplace culture in Springfield that's too often toxic and harmful. We need a plan to make things better. I've been talking with my colleagues throughout the summer, and I'm hopeful that we can come together in veto session with some concrete steps to improve our processes and keep our people safe.”</p><p>Rep. Ann Stava, D-Naperville, noted that the working group got off to a very rocky start: “[Welch’s] response was to formally assign people to a working group to ‘study the issue.’ Multiple members who were assigned declined to join for reasons they specified publicly.”</p><p>Stava also said that she hadn’t decided whether to vote for Welch in January, and warned, “I do not look kindly on the fact that he has not personally apologized to the original victim or the subsequent victims to my knowledge.”</p><p>In my own opinion, Welch should follow through on both of his public promises: Genuinely apologize and improve the staff working environment.</p><p>Instead, the House Democrats have gone on offense against the Republican candidate running against Benton's successor, Gabby Shanahan.</p><p>Benton was succeeded by one of his former district office employees, who said she witnessed Benton's sexual harassment but didn't report it because the young staffer asked her not to. The Republicans have sharply and repeatedly criticized appointed Rep. entries.title: Nelson Wendell's four TDs and 355 total yards leads Geneva past Batavia
entries.summary: <p>Geneva and Batavia have been playing each other in football since 1913, but they've never had a game quite like this.</p><p>With multiple Division prospects on both sides fueling a pair of high-powered offenses, No. 16 Geneva held on for a wild 56-49 road win over No 6 Batavia Friday night in front of a standing-room-only crowd.</p><p>Nelson Wendell, who missed last year's game with a broken foot, ran for 303 yards for Geneva (5-1, 4-0 DuKane) and turned a screen pass from Ben Peterson into a 49-yard touchdown that put the Vikings ahead to stay with 1:04 left in the game. He finished with four TDs and 355 total yards.</p><p>For Batavia (4-2, 3-1), quarterback Michael Vander Luitgaren accounted for 495 total yards (291 passing and 204 rushing) and seven touchdowns (three rushing and four passing).</p><p>"There's so much history between these towns," said Vander Luitgaren, a Wyoming commit. "... You want to play in the Batavia/Geneva rivalry game and it didn't disappoint. All the fans showed up — they showed out and they were loud. There were some plays on offense where I'm surprised some of the guys heard me out there. Credit to Geneva fans, they were super loud. Credit to our fans."</p><p>Wendell started coming to the game long before he could play in it, when his dad was an assistant football coach at Geneva.</p><p>Winning it "means everything," he said. "I feel like this is the biggest game of the year, so it's really great to get it done and for the community."</p><p>The game was like a track meet most of the way. There were just two punts total, and eight of the first nine possessions in the second half ended with touchdowns. That included fwo Batavia TDs in a 15-second span of the fourth quarter when the Bulldogs rallied from two scores down to tie it at 49 with 3:23 remaining.</p><p>Vander Luitgaren threw a 37-yard TD to Western Michigan commit Darin Ashiru, Batavia recovered an onside kick and Vander Luitgaren zigged and zagged his way to a 52-yard TD run. Ashiru had 11 catches for 147 yards and two TDs.</p><p>"He's a hell of a football player," Wendell, who started on defense for the first time all season, said of Vander Luitgaren. "I was diving at his ankles the whole game and missed a lot of tackles. He's going to be so special when he goes to college."</p><p>But Wendell had one more big play of his own to put Geneva back in front to stay.</p><p>On second-and-14 from the Batavia 49, the Vikings ran a screen to the right side.</p><p>"It was the perfect play call," Wendell said. "They sent three guys on a full blitz."</p><p>Peterson dumped the ball off to Wendell and he followed his blockers into the end zone. Batavia's last drive ended in a turnover on downs at its own 44, Peterson took a knee and Geneva had its second win in three years in the series. The Vikings lead it 53-50 with five ties.</p><p>Peterson, an Eastern Michigan commit, was 14 of 23 passing for 233 yards and three touchdowns with one interception. He also had 10 carries for 60 yards and two TDs. Illinois recruit Bennett Konkey had six catches for 76 yards and a score.</p><p>"Me and Mike [Vander Luitgaren] have always had great games," Peterson said. "He got the best of us last year and I give Mike so many props. ... Batavia has a really, really, really good team and I think they're going to make a really big run in [Class] 7A because of Mike."</p><p>And Peterson expects a long postseason run for Geneva in 6A,</p><p>"I think we have a very similar team to the one that went to state two years ago, and I think that all the pieces are lining up," he said. "We beat [Batavia] on their home field two years ago and I think we have another team that can make it back to state as well."</p>

entries.title: Northwestern puts a scare into No. 5 Indiana
entries.summary: <p>BLOOMINGTON, Ind. — Indiana running back Lee Beebe Jr. waited a whole year for an opportunity like the one he got Friday night.</p><p>And with starting running back Turbo Richard out with an injury, Beebe gladly showed everyone what he could do.</p><p>On a night the Hoosiers looked nothing like the defending national champs, Beebe carried 24 times for 203 yards, scored one touchdown and his late 70-yard burst set up Josh Hoover's game-sealing 1-yard score with 1:56 to go as No. 5 Indiana held on for a 29-23 victory over Northwestern. Beebe was so good, he even earned the highest praise from coach Curt Cignetti.</p><p>“That guy’s got a lot of heart,” Cignetti said. “Boy, he’s got as much heart as anyone that’s been in this program the last three years. Not only didn’t he step in, he played and fortunately they couldn’t tackle him. It was all grit and heart.”</p><p>The Hoosiers (4-0, 1-0 Big Ten) extended the Football Bowl Subdivision's longest active winning streak to 20 games and the longest home winning streak to 19 — barely.</p><p>Northwestern was within 15-13 early in the fourth quarter and had two chances to tie because of a pass-interference call on its first 2-point attempt. But the Hoosiers stopped quarterback Aidan Chiles on a designed run to preserve the lead.</p><p>Following a facemask penalty on third-and-19 that gave Indiana a first down, Beebe ripped off a 39-yard run and then ran for a 4-yard TD with 9:39 left to make it a two-score game. After Northwestern cut the deficit to 22-20, Beebe ran 70 yards to the Wildcats 5-yard line. Six plays later, Hoover scored.</p><p>Northwestern fell just short of beating a defending national champion for the first time since 1971 and a top five foe for the first time since 1959.</p><p>“Our guys kept battling, our coaches kept battling, but the frustrating thing was — I have all the respect for Indiana — but we beat ourselves,” Wildcats coach David Braun said. “We should be coming out of here with the win.”</p><p>They certainly had Indiana befuddled in the second half, right down to the final minute.</p><p>Jackson Kleather made a 42-yard field goal with 58 seconds left to make it a one-score game, but the Wildcats (2-1, 0-1) couldn't recover the onside kick.</p><p>Hoover was 19 of 29 for 201 yards and a touchdown, Charlie Becker had seven catches for 98 yards and Beebe had his second 100-yard game of the season after Turbo Richard left with a lower right leg injury in the first half.</p><p>Chiles was 22 of 29 for 293 yards and touchdowns. He also rushed for a score.</p><p>The Wildcats opened the game with a goal-line stand, but Chiles fumbled the snap on their first offensive play and Rolijah Hardy tackled him in the end zone for a safety.</p><p>Indiana made it 5-0 on Nico Radicic's 43-yard field goal early in the second quarter and extended the margin to 12-0 with Nick Marsh's 8-yard TD catch with 5:04 left in the first half.</p><p>But that's all the Hoosiers could muster in a half in which they held Northwestern to 51 total yards and minus-5 yards on the ground.</p><p><b>The takeaway</b></p><p>Northwestern: The Wildcats couldn't get anything right offensively in the first half, but coordinator Chip Kelly turned Chiles loose in the second half and it got them back into the game. The failed 2-point try and the defense's failure to get off the field coast them late.</p><p>Indiana: Poll voters penalized the Hoosiers last week, dropping them one spot after a 38-0 rout of Western Kentucky. And this was as vulnerable as Indiana's defense has looked in more than a year. Whether it's an aberration is unclear, but it's likely the Hoosiers will drop in the AP Top 25 again.</p><p><b>Injury report</b></p><p>Richard appeared to suffer a lower right leg injury when he was tackled out of bounds in the second quarter though no penalty was called. Indiana is also missing RB Khobie Martin with a broken arm. The Hoosiers also lost linebacker Hardy in the second half, and he walked from the field straight to the locker room. Cignetti did not provide any postgame updates.</p><p>Northwestern played without injured cornerback Braden Turner and lost cornerback Josh Fussell on the game’s first series. He was in street clothes and on crutches before the first quarter ended. Chiles also left for one play after he apparently suffered a dislocated finger on his nonthrowing hand.</p><p><b>Up next</b></p><p>Northwestern: Has another big test next Saturday, hosting No. 13 Penn State.</p><p>Indiana: Visits winless Rutgers next Saturday in its first away game of the season.</p>

entries.title: White Sox' Munetaka Murakami getting hot at perfect time, homers twice in win
entries.summary: <p>White Sox first baseman Munetaka Murakami had 54 at-bats against Rockies right-hander Tomoyuki Sugano in Japan's Nippon Professional Baseball. Sugano largely owned Murakami, holding him to a .204 batting average. But Murakami took him deep twice.</p><p>In their first meeting in Major League Baseball on Friday, Murakami also took him deep twice.</p><p>“Mune” hit his 34th homer in the first inning and his 35th in the seventh, solo shots that helped the Sox beat the Rockies 6-1 at Rate Field. Murakami, who added an RBI single in the eighth, is getting hot at the perfect time as the Sox try to catch the Guardians in the American League Central and build momentum heading into the postseason.</p><p>In his last eight games, Murakami has an OPS of 1.272 with four homers and 12 RBI. He became the second Japanese-born player in MLB history with at least 35 homers in a season, joining the Dodgers’ Shohei Ohtani (four times). He also joined Jose Abreu (36 in 2014) and Ron Kittle (35 in 1983) as the only Sox rookies to hit 35-plus homers in a season.</p><p>“It’s right on time, and it’s great to see,” manager Will Venable said. “We know how impactful he can be when he’s right and feeling good. Smushing some baseballs today, which was great to see. The contact from him — if he hits it, he’s going to hit hard.”</p><p>And he can hit it anywhere. His first homer went 386 feet to right field; his second went 412 feet to center. He also has been known to hit some to the opposite field. In fact, 29% of Murakami’s homers have gone to center, left-center or left; the rest have gone to right-center or right.</p><p>“He’s such a tough AB when he’s rolling like he is,” said right-hander Sean Burke, the beneficiary of Murakami’s blasts. “You see two balls launched, one pull side, one oppo. Just the power he has, he’s such a dangerous bat.”</p><p>He might be a bit more dangerous than he has been. Murakami said he has been working on his lower-body strength in the last two weeks in his never-ending pursuit of improvement.</p><p>“It’s not like I haven’t been doing any lower-body strengthening,” he said through an interpreter. “It’s more evolving. I’m adding on to something that is needed at the moment because the body changes. It lessens the other things that I have to worry about, so I’m able to focus on the at-bats more.”</p><p>As for beating Sugano, Murakami wasn’t about to gloat.</p><p>“Sugano has been in the majors for quite a while,” Murakami said. “Yes, we had our matchups in the past, but it was different, and I was able to pull through today.”</p>

entries.summary: <p>Mount Carmel vs. Brother Rice is not a normal high school football game. Not this season.</p><p>The Caravan won Class 8A last year and entered the season as the most talented and hyped high school football team in area history.</p><p>The host Crusaders won Class 7A last season and feature multiple major Power Five recruits, including defensive end Kameron McGee, who some scouts consider the best prospect in the country in the junior class.</p><p>To add to the spectacle, a Chicago Police Department helicopter did a flyover after the National Anthem. entries.title: Now more than ever, cancel culture is no game
entries.summary: <p>'‘That little monkey gets loose, doesn’t he?”</p><p>The silencing of Howard Cosell could be looked at as the modern-day beginning when he, on ‘‘MNF,’’ got caught up in his own insolence to describe Washington wide receiver Alvin Garrett’s speed and stature and elusiveness during a breakaway run for the end zone.</p><p>A decade before that, Cosell unintentionally said during a highlight segment about another black player: “Look at that little monkey run.”</p><p>Canceled.</p><p>“No, I don’t believe it’s prejudice. I truly believe that they may not have some of the, uh, necessities, uh, to be, uh, let’s say, a field manager or perhaps a general manager. . . . Well, I don’t say that all of them, but they certainly are short. How many quarterbacks do you have, how many pitchers do you have that are Black? . . . No, it’s not garbage, Mr. Koppel. . . . Why are Black men or Black people not good swimmers? Because they don’t have the buoyancy.”</p><p>Dodgers general manager Al Campanis spoke his truth in 1987 to Ted Koppel on ‘‘Nightline.’’ Speaking on the lack of black managers in the majors 40 years after Jackie Robinson had entered the National League. His reasoning didn’t go over well.</p><p>Canceled.</p><p>Twenty-nine years later, NFL quarterback Colin Kaepernick went down on one knee in protest of the excessive police killing of black men. He decided to do this during the playing of the national anthem at NFL games. The country took issue. The country divided over the issue. “Wouldn’t you love to see one of these NFL owners, when somebody disrespects our flag, to say, ‘Get that son of a bitch off the field right now. Out! He’s fired. He’s fired!’ ’’ is what the president of the United States said. “I think we’ve moved past kneeling, and I think it’s time to go into actionable items” is how Jay-Z put it upon his partnership with the NFL. As for Kaepernick and the power behind his protest . . .</p><p>Canceled.</p><p>There has been a long history of cancel culture and its relationship both within and with sports. Mostly flashpoint moments. Isolated incidents that often detonate. “The suppression of freedom of expression,” critical realist and sociologist David Pilgrim calls it. How “neoliberal individualism has enabled recent forms of silencing and punishment” and become what we now see as society’s most current version of cancel culture.</p><p>Making the most recent wave of cancelable incidents connected to sports triggering.</p><p>Patriots owner Robert Kraft decided to give Ed Sheeran the ultimate ultimatum. Everyone canceled Sheeran, but no one canceled the Patriots despite the fact that it was the team’s owner who initiated the petulant demand.</p><p>Shaquille O’Neal accepts an award from FBI director Kash Patel, and now Shaq has been the subject of a whole cancellation vibe that’s worse than Patel got when he tried to cancel the “deep state.”</p><p>The NBA canceled Steve Ballmer before the public had an opportunity to over the salary-cap scandal. But Pablo Torre came out like a king. Jay-Z’s “we’re past kneeling” came back to haunt him after his Yankee Stadium residency rant about Kaepernick. While the full-on cancel button wasn’t pushed when it came to Jay-Z, his “black card” (for that and other reasons) is inching closer to revokable status.</p><p>How about the Good Good Golf and Callaway “domestic violence” campaign? The Golf Channel pulled the plug on their reality-show partnership, and Dick’s Sporting Goods pulled all of Good Good’s product from their shelves and off their sites. Novig’s “sexualized devaluation of women athletes and athletics” ad featuring the strategically nude Sydney Sweeney saying “sport” or “sports” 16 times during a 58-second commercial. (One that caused the company to have a 151% rise on their Instagram account.) Allowed yet disavowed.</p><p>Lane Kiffin and the NCAA. LeBron James and his recent Polymarket partnership. Sophie Cunningham and the left. Cunningham and her rumored boyfriend. ESPN and Ted Cruz. Mark Walter, private equity and modern professional sports franchise ownership.</p><p>Cancel. Cancel. Cancel. Cancel.</p><p>Then there’s the Converse ad. The sneaker brand owned by Nike. In a campaign that took on a life of its own when someone cropped a still image from their latest campaign that unintentionally depicted the image of a KKK hood and the “black” feet dangle of someone hanging alongside the hood silhouette. One of those “once you see it, you can’t unsee it” images. One of those “how did no one at Converse or Nike or at the ad agency not catch this” incidents. One of those “unintentional or intentional” doesn’t even matter moments.</p><p>There is a difference between getting canceled and getting clowned. What and what can’t be written off as an accident or coincidence. That thin line between what we decide to tolerate against what we choose to cancel. Identity politics. Enragement vs. engagement. Where the messages are no longer subliminal. The Tik-Tokification of everything. Where algorithms run all things. All at the intersection of polarization and accountability.</p><p>Sports now stands at the forefront.</p><p>Nuance and narrative. The public shaming and community retribution that comes when one participates in the drama they create. Sports always has occupied some space in the cancel-culture ethos, but recently it seems to have gone rogue in a way not seen since Jim Thorpe met Jim Crow.</p><p>Now that we’re at this hypersensitive inflection extremity, I’ll ask, can canceling be canceled?</p>

entries.title: Rookie Caleb Wilson is the headliner in Bulls camp, but he's not alone
entries.summary: <p>The headliner isn’t a question.</p><p>When Bulls camp tips off Monday with media day, all eyes — fair or unfair — will be on rookie Caleb Wilson.</p><p>Since becoming the No. 4 overall pick in a loaded 2026 draft in June, Wilson has talked it and walked it with very few missteps. He was must-see TV in Summer League, he has been in the lab on a daily basis working on his game with teammates and with members of his Klutch Sports -family, and he has shown a likable bravado that has become endearing throughout the city.</p><p>There’s no doubt that Wilson is the future.</p><p>But there is a present.</p><p>That’s the reality that will hit the organization in the face with the ferocity of a Wilson dunk.</p><p>See, hype and hope are nice. They sell, especially in a city like Chicago. At some point, however, the games start up and they count. The Bulls do have four players ranked in the ESPN 100 that was just released, which is a nice foundation for a rebuild, but not one player is above No. 80 Josh Giddey.</p><p>New Bulls veteran Norman Powell was No. 86, Matas Buzelis was No. 88 and Wilson was No. 97.</p><p>Victor Wembanyama and the loaded young Spurs can sleep easy tonight.</p><p>What that means is while the Bulls new-look front office has acknowledged that this is a rebuild, there are going to be some painful nights for this group that test hype and hope. Maybe they exceed the Las Vegas win total of 27 ½ to 29 ½ wins, but even a 32-win season is still a lot of ugly.</p><p>That’s where Wilson (20 years old) — and to a certain extent Buzelis (21) — come in. If the tandem can become a problem for teams on both ends of the floor and the rest of the roster just isn’t good enough to sniff Eastern Conference play-in territory, the rebuild will at least have traction moving forward.</p><p>Big ifs that will start being answered this week.</p><p>Top five camp storylines</p><p><b>1. For starters</b> — Mapping out the starting lineup is as chalky as it has been for the Bulls in a few seasons. Giddey and Powell will man the backcourt, while Nic Claxton, Buzelis and Wilson will hold down the frontcourt. The good news for this group? For the most part, four of the starters — Wilson is the unknown — have showcased the best ability to have — availability.</p><p>Even Claxton, who has been working through back issues the last few seasons, played 69 games for the Nets last season and 70 the season before that.</p><p><b>2. French connection</b> — Even with Noa Essengue’s rookie season basically being a redshirt year because of his shoulder surgery, there is still a lot for the 6-11 forward to prove. Not only does he need to show up for camp with an improved physicality, but he needs to show Tiago Splitter and the coaching staff that he can be emotionally mature when things don’t go his way on the floor.</p><p>This front office and coaching staff didn’t draft Essengue No. 12 overall in 2025. They have no allegiance to him. That also means they won’t bend over backwards to accommodate a player that isn’t ready to pull the rope.</p><p><b>3. Battleground</b> — While the starters are basically set, there are reserve spots still to be won. Tre Jones, Isaac Okoro, Jalen Smith and Zach Collins — when healthy — are all in as far as the makeup of the second unit. That leaves Rob Dillingham and rookie -Dailyn Swain trying to etch out backcourt playing time, while Patrick Williams, Essengue and Leonard Miller will battle for frontcourt minutes.</p><p>Based on last season, Miller should have the lead because of the way he finished the year, but with a new staff, each player is back to equal ground.</p><p><b>4. Speaking of Swain</b> — It was beyond rough for the rookie in Summer League as his shot betrayed him and his ball-handling skills were shaky at best. But Swain was picked No. 15 out of Texas for a reason and these preseason games will be a huge opportunity to put Las Vegas and Summer League behind him.</p><p><b>5. The Tiago effect</b> — Splitter maybe had the best coaching season of anyone last year, taking over the Trail Blazers when then-coach Chauncey Billups was pinched by the feds for allegedly rigging card games. All Splitter did was take Portland to a win in a play-in game and a berth in the postseason.</p><p>Is he a true miracle worker? That will be tested with this group, starting with what kind of culture he wants established. Does this roster have the pieces in place for those seeds to start growing? A big ask that will lead eventually to answers.</p>

entries.title: Why Ian Cole is a 'really good match' with the Blackhawks
entries.summary: <p>Ian Cole helped create Landon Slaggert's earliest hockey memory.</p><p>The new <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/blackhawks" target="_blank" >Blackhawks</a> defenseman, now 37, was a 19-year-old freshman when Notre Dame made a dramatic run through the 2008 NCAA tournament to the national championship game, which they lost to Boston College.</p><p>Slaggert, now 24, was a six-year-old kid at the time, scrambling around the locker room while his dad Andy, an assistant coach, did his job. </p><p>To him, those Fighting Irish players were his "superheroes." Cole remembers Slaggert as an even younger kid while he was being recruited to Notre Dame, too.</p><p>Now, they're Hawks teammates.</p><p>"[It's] a little weird," Slaggert said Friday, smiling. "I'm kind of hitting a quarter-life crisis. But it's pretty sweet, honestly."</p><p>It would probably be weirder if they hadn't seen each other plenty of times at Notre Dame events in recent years, but they have. They know each other well now.</p><p>Cole, for that matter, knows many people around the hockey world well. That's inevitable for a personable guy who just joined his 10th different franchise in his 17th NHL season.</p><p>He and Frank Nazar share the same agent, Kevin Magnuson. He and Teuvo Teravainen played together on the Hurricanes in 2021-22. The next season, he was coached by then-Lightning assistant coach Jeff Blashill in Tampa.</p><p>Those "known quantities" gave Cole comfort when he decided to sign a one-year, $4 million contract with the Hawks on July 1.</p><p>"I'm a big fan of how [Blashill] handles the team and the spotlight and how he runs things," Cole said. "He does a really great job."</p><p>He has enjoyed familiarizing himself with rest of the young Hawks, including defenseman Sam Rinzel, who was four years old when Cole went to college yet has skated as his regular partner throughout training camp.</p><p>Their collective "youthful exuberance" has been refreshing, putting aside the fact they never understand his movie references.</p><p>"The guys are young, yes, but everyone wants to get better...and everyone wants to be a playoff team," Cole said. "I think everyone here believes that we can do that."</p><p>Cole's teams have made the playoffs in 12 of his first 16 seasons, including Stanley Cup wins with the Penguins in 2016 and 2017, so he has plenty of relevant firsthand experience to share. </p><p>That hasn't happened much yet inside the locker room, but he expects it will as the season progresses. One occasion that will likely prompt a discussion: Cole will hit the 1,000-game milestone after just 10 games with the Hawks, possibly (barring injury) as soon as Oct. 23.</p><p>His most recent playoff berth came last season with the Mammoth — a young-in-their-own-right team that the Hawks actually swept in their four-game season series, giving Cole a glimpse of the Hawks' potential before he joined them.</p><p>"Last year, I think they had the ability to beat anyone on any given day and also potentially lose to anyone on any given day," he said. </p><p>"My read of the situation...is if we can clean up some of those things that caused us to lose games, we'll put ourselves in a very good position to continue to climb those standings."</p><p>Cole essentially replaces Connor Murphy as the elder statesman of the Hawks' defense and a staple of their penalty kill. Slaggert, who obviously knows Murphy well, agreed their "calming presence" is similar.</p><p>"Ian does a really good job of managing risk-reward," Blashill said. "[He] knows when there’s a play to be made and when there’s not. [He] doesn’t try to make something up that’s not there. [He] really understands what he’s good at and does that.</p><p>"He’s got a maturity to his game. And if there’s an area that all young players have to improve at, that would be the maturity of their game. ... It makes [him] a really good match for our group."</p>

entries.title: How we photographed Bears QB Caleb Williams' hamstring injury
entries.summary: <p>This week’s top photo comes from Visual Journalist Manuel Martinez. Follow him on <a class="Link" href="https://www.instagram.com/nueli/" target="_blank" >Instagram</a>.</p><h3>What makes this photo important?</h3><p>Sports photography isn’t just capturing the action, but often more importantly about telling the story of emotion both in moments of triumph and defeat. The quarterback is said to be the most important player on the football field. Bears quarterback Caleb Williams' job is not only to make the plays, but to carry the team on his shoulders with the hope each week of leading them to a win. When Williams scrambled toward the end zone during the fourth quarter Sunday, I knew I was about to shoot an important play, but what came next was unexpected. When he fell, the stadium went from pure joy to total silence. The image captures the heavy price of playing a violent sport, but also Williams' willingness to put his body at risk for a win. The season rides on the health of the team, so losing the star quarterback was tragic. It’s not always easy bearing witness to these heavy moments, but it also reminds us that sports are a mixture of joy and disappointment.</p><h3>How I got this photo:</h3><p>Talk about getting your feet wet! This image was shot during the season home opener for the Bears in a five-hour rain storm. Sports photography requires skill, patience and a whole lot of luck. The rain was relentless from the moment that my colleague and I arrived at Soldier Field, to the moment we left. Everything I was carrying was soaked within the first 30 minutes, and it made shooting difficult. I was positioned on the right side of the field, behind the end zone. Williams ran directly towards me and, what I figured would be a touchdown image, turned out to be a game-ending injury image. Everything in sports happens so fast you really don’t have time to think, it is a very instinctual form of photography. I was relying on all of my years of experience and instinct to try to capture a difficult moment for Williams and his team. The image almost doesn’t need a caption because you can feel his pain and imagine how every Bears fan felt watching their leader fall.</p><h3></h3><h3><b>Technical details:</b></h3><ul entries.title: Life insurance protects dependent loved ones
entries.summary: <p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/news/2026/08/25/dolly-parton-music-star-actor-and-beloved-figure-who-spanned-generations-has-died-at-80" >Dolly Parton</a> built an extraordinary legacy. Through her music, business ventures and philanthropy she created something that will continue to touch people’s lives long after her recent death. Her story is a reminder that a legacy is not just about what we accomplish during our lifetime — it is also about what we leave behind for the people we love.</p><p>For most of us, that legacy begins much closer to home: making sure our families will be financially secure if we are no longer there to provide for them.</p><p>Planning for the future is not always easy, especially with the demands we face today: raising children, working full time or going to school, managing everyday expenses, caring for our own health, and for many, supporting aging relatives.</p><p>Yet the need to plan is real. A recent study found that more than 40% of U.S. households say they don’t have adequate financial resources to protect their children if the primary wage earner were to die.</p><p>One of the most effective ways to provide that protection is life insurance. It is an important and often affordable tool for safeguarding the people we love and helping provide financial security for the future. Life insurance can replace lost income, pay a mortgage, fund a child’s education and provide stability when families are already facing tremendous emotional loss.</p><p>September is Life Insurance Awareness Month, making it a good time to take a fresh look at whether your financial safety net is strong enough to protect your family’s dreams and build legacies. Start the conversation with your spouse or partner and then talk to a qualified life insurance professional about options that may be appropriate for your circumstances.</p><p>The impact of life insurance is significant right here in Illinois. Life insurers paid $5.62 billion in benefits to Illinois families in 2024. Nearly 6 million Illinois residents already have some life insurance coverage, with an average death benefit of approximately $171,000.</p><p>Life insurance is ultimately about more than a policy or financial product. It is about protecting the people who depend on you and preserving the plans you have made for their future. It ensures that the legacy you have worked so hard to build can continue, even when life takes an unexpected turn.</p><p><i>Laura Minzer, president, Illinois Life & Health Insurance Council</i></p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-670000" name="module-670000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>Give us your take</h3><br>Send letters to the editor to <a class="Link" href="mailto:letters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" >letters@suntimes.com</a>. To be considered for publication, letters must include your full name, your neighborhood or hometown and a phone number for verification purposes. Letters should be a maximum of approximately 375 words.</div> </div><p></p><h3>Philanthropists can give more to protect immigrants</h3><p>It's been a year since <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bearing-the-blitz/2026/09/08/how-operation-midway-blitz-played-out" >Operation Midway Blitz </a>began, and U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents are still present in Chicago. That said, <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/in-the-loop-with-sasha-ann-simons/2026/09/01/a-year-after-midway-blitz-community-members-reflect-on-efforts-to-protect-each-other-from-ice-aggression" target="_blank" >immigration enforcement tactics</a> have changed. <a class="Link" href="https://ilac.illinois.gov/commission-updates/2026-04-30-iac-issues-final-report-release.html" target="_blank" ><u>Public neighborhood raids</u></a> have been <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/the-rundown-chicago-news-podcast/2026/09/08/special-episode-bearing-witness-to-the-blitz" target="_blank" ><u>replaced by quick, targeted maneuvers</u></a>.</p><p>So far this year, <a class="Link" href="https://www.openimmigration.us/enforcement" target="_blank" ><u>ICE deported</u></a> more than 350,000 people — many who were <a class="Link" href="https://www.chicagotribune.com/2025/09/18/day-laborers-chicago-ice/" target="_blank" ><u>abducted while working</u></a> or <a class="Link" href="https://www.newsweek.com/ice-accused-of-arresting-parents-at-school-bus-stops-12373461" target="_blank" ><u>taking their children to school.</u></a> Multiple reports indicate that men, women and children detained in ICE facilities face<a class="Link" href="https://immigrantjustice.org/research/after-the-blitz-what-our-chicago-neighbors-are-facing-in-detention/" target="_blank" ><u> inhumane conditions and due process violations</u></a>. And, most horrifyingly, an average of one person a week <a class="Link" href="https://www.democracynow.org/2026/4/21/ice_custody_deaths_ghandehari_detention_watch" target="_blank" ><u>dies in ICE custody</u></a>.</p><p>The horrors caused by the Trump administration’s anti-immigrant policies have led many to ask what we can do to support communities most affected. As a refugee policy scholar and a <a class="Link" href="https://www.wieboldt.org/" target="_blank" >Wieboldt Foundation</a> board member, I see the urgency of this moment and an opportunity for philanthropy to meet it.</p><p>Funders should consider unrestricted grants to organizations with track records of effectively building trust and serving directly impacted communities, including the <a class="Link" href="https://immigrantjustice.org/" target="_blank" >National Immigrant Justice Center</a>, <a class="Link" href="https://www.icirr.org/" target="_blank" >Illinois Coalition for Immigrant and Refugee Rights</a>, <a class="Link" href="https://refugeeone.org/" target="_blank" ><u>RefugeeOne</u></a> and <a class="Link" href="https://worldrelief.org/chicagoland/homepage/" target="_blank" ><u>World Relief</u></a>. Philanthropy is already an important partner to these agencies. But the scale of need has grown. The proliferation of federal anti-immigration policies is not letting up. So more funding is needed now.</p><p>Philanthropy also has a unique role to play in bolstering immigration defense by supporting community organizing, which is the most effective strategy for community self-determination. When neighbors come together to share concerns and envision solutions to the challenges they face, they are building political power — this is democracy in action. Front-line groups like the <a class="Link" href="https://www.csplaction.org/" target="_blank" >Coalition for Spiritual & Public Leadership</a> and <a class="Link" href="https://www.organizedcommunities.org/about" target="_blank" >Organized Communities Against Defense</a> have been in the streets organizing people across the city. For those who are unsure about how best to support targeted communities, these organizations offer an opportunity for us to listen and learn.</p><p>Philanthropy has a crucial role in immigration defense. Partnership with immigrant communities will demonstrate our commitment to a democracy in which everyone is valued. The impact of our financial support for services and grassroots community organizing will be immediate and lasting.</p><p><i>Jessica Darrow, associate instructional professor, University of Chicago Crown Family School of Social Work, Policy, and Practice and board member, Wieboldt Foundation</i></p><h3>NU isn’t upholding African studies program legacy</h3><p>I graduated from Northwestern University in June. As the whirlwind of seemingly endless graduation events subsided, I found myself thinking about who I was when I applied to Northwestern and who I had become by the time I left Evanston.</p><p>To understand the person I had become, I decided to revisit the ambitions of the 17-year-old me who had written Northwestern’s supplemental essays. In one of the essays, I wrote about a professor who specialized in African studies.</p><p>After enrolling in the university, I saw that the professor I had written about was teaching a course on African politics. I enrolled.</p><p>The professor invited me to attend a department open house. We walked along the main street of campus until we reached a house that was tucked away behind trees and a wooden sign that displayed the inscription, “Program of African Studies.”</p><p>I began working at the program of African studies soon after the open house. I would often browse through the books, as it allowed me to immerse myself in the long lineage of African studies at Northwestern.</p><p>“The history of studies about Africa in this country is intimately bound up with the study of Africa at Northwestern," Gwendolen M. Carter, a former African studies director, wrote in an essay in the 1974 issue of The Pan-Africanist — a now defunct Northwestern student publication.</p><p>Carter's statement reflected the university’s pioneering role in the field as Northwestern became the first university in the United States to formalize a program devoted to the study of Africa in 1948.</p><p>Last month, nearly 80 years later, Northwestern announced that the program will be transitioning away from its status as a universitywide research institute and center.</p><p>Northwestern maintains that the African studies program is not closing. Yet the university has eliminated its remaining two staff positions and has provided few details about where the program will be housed or what will happen to its funding.</p><p>The <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/other-views/2026/08/26/northwestern-african-studies-black-america-ryan-field-jeffrey-sterling" >African studies program </a>created spaces that allowed students to encounter Africa not simply through headlines about the troubles afflicting African countries, but through the continent’s languages, histories, cultures and people.</p><p>By stripping its African studies program of its status as a research center, Northwestern is sending a clear message about which human experiences are deemed worthy of serious inquiry.</p><p><i>Mariam Cosmos, Washington, D.C.</i></p><h3>Chicagoans don’t need another gambling options </h3><p>Not only is legalizing video gambling terminals "a bad bet" for Chicago, as John Bosca and Julie Darling wrote in their recent <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/other-views/2026/09/23/legalizing-video-gambling-terminals-is-a-bad-bet-for-chicago" >op-ed</a>, it will also victimize Chicagoans. </p><p>Too many Chicagoans are already spending money they cannot afford to lose on Illinois Lottery's Lotto games, Red Hot Millions, etc., tickets that can be purchased at the countless gas stations and convenience stores scattered around the Chicago area. The City Council now enables these same folks to gamble and drink alcohol at the same time?</p><p>Those alderpersons who are brave enough to try to reverse the legalization of gaming machines in bars would be acting in the best interests of their ward members.</p><p><i>Terry Takash, Western Springs</i></p><h3>Dangers of AI </h3><h3></h3><p>Artificial intelligence is not a living entity. AI is made using computer code to create mathematical models capable of being trained by the input of massive amounts of data allowing the models to recognize patterns and make predictions and eventually take actions.</p><p>The danger of these AI models is a direct result of the intents of the humans who create them. Many of these AI models are being created by the same people who created the social media programs currently causing unforeseen social damage. AI models only attempt to escape their so-called "playpens" if such directives are embedded in the models via coding.</p><p>We waited too late to learn about social media. We should not wait to set guardrails for AI. If you think social media is a problem, then uncontrolled AI will be catastrophic </p><p><i>Warren Rodgers Jr., Orland Park</i></p><h3>Trump’s problematic pledge </h3><p>Earlier this month, Donald Trump offered <a class="Link" href="https://apnews.com/article/trump-dividend-5k-5000-check-republicans-cc80644e3168acd31c892129fb849436" target="_blank" >$5,000</a> to all American adults if Republicans maintain control of the House and Senate. Almost immediately a debate began about whether this proposal constitutes a bribe.</p><p>Some legal experts say no, because the payment will be available to every adult, regardless of how they vote. Others, however, contend that the very essence of a bribe is to induce people to engage in actions or behaviors they would not have otherwise engaged in.</p><p>Either way, this proposed payment will bring devastating results to the economy. The national debt is at a record high, topping <a class="Link" href="https://www.npr.org/2026/08/19/nx-s1-5937552/the-u-s-debt-tops-a-record-shattering-40-trillion-yes-with-a-t" target="_blank" >$40 trillion</a> for the first time in history. These projected payouts themselves, given America’s adult population, would add more than a trillion dollars to this debt.</p><p>Conversely, if Republicans do regain control of the House and Senate, Trump could then renege on his promise, or it could get invalidated by the courts. By this time many Americans may have made credit purchases or refinanced loans based on this anticipated payout, meaning the personal debt they would not have otherwise incurred, but for Trump’s promise, will also negatively impact the economy.</p><p>Out of all the tricks the Republicans have employed to impact the midterms — from gerrymandering based on race (but calling it political), to threatening to prosecute election officials, to intimidating polling places — this may be their apex.</p><p>When I say Republicans, I speak in general terms, because there are still some Republicans who place the good of the nation over the whims of their cult leader. But at this point, you can count them on one hand and still have some fingers left over.</p><p><i>David R. Hoffman, retired civil rights and constitutional law attorney, South Bend, Indiana</i></p><h3>Stable genius? </h3><p>In what world can the president of the United States bar reporters from the White House because he does not like what they report and a couple days later announce to the entire world he may have to <a class="Link" href="https://www.nbcnews.com/politics/trump-administration/trump-address-united-nations-general-assembly-iran-war-rcna599085" target="_blank" >annihilate</a> a country?</p><p><i>Mike Sienkowski, Tinley Park</i></p><h3>Bracing for holy vengeance in postseason play </h3><p>So, there's good news and bad in both the Cubs and White Sox making the playoffs. As for the good, this fall will now have even more to offer than pumpkin spice lattes and cider doughnuts. </p><p>But on the other hand, we have to brace ourselves for a reckoning if <br>Nostradamus predicted no American pope will ever wave a championship banner out his Vatican window.</p><p><i>Bob Ory, Elgin</i><br></p>

entries.title: Call me a proponent of keeping cellphones out of classrooms
entries.summary: <p>Last month I attended Jill Scott’s concert at The Chicago Theatre for her “To Whom It May Concern Tour.” The neo-soul chanteuse implemented a strict no-cellphone policy. At the doorway, ushers handed out pouches to secure any device that could record. After the show, they were unlocked. The same process happened at the same theater when I saw one of my favorite R&B groups, Tony! Toni! Tone! Artists want concertgoers to soak in the music and be locked in to the performances.</p><p>The policy worked. Listening in a communal space without a blue-screen glare or people distractingly posting live on Instagram elevated the concert. Much of life these days is documenting and proving fun. If it’s not online, it didn’t happen.</p><p>Those cellphone-free, concert-going experiences make me think about the new Illinois cellphone ban in public schools. In July, Gov. JB Pritzker <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/springfield/2026/07/28/illinois-school-cellphone-ban-signed-law-jb-pritzker" >signed a law</a> that bans cellphones and personal devices in classrooms. Deeper connections and less distractions in the classroom are the dual goals. The bell-to-bell policy for kindergarten through eighth grade includes lunch and passing periods. For high schools, access could be allowed during passing periods or lunch. This year the state board of education shared a template policy for school districts, and at the start of next academic year a plan must be implemented. </p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-floatRight><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-f00000" name="module-f00000"></a> <div class="RichTextSidebarModule-title">Columnist </div> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h2>Columnists</h2></div> </div><p>A list of exceptions range from medical to caregiving. But the bottom line is teachers are sick of competing with cellphones and accompanying social media. Illinois joins nearly two dozen states that have enacted some sort of <a class="Link" href="https://www.hks.harvard.edu/faculty-research/policy-topics/education-training-labor/many-states-are-banning-cellphones-schools" target="_blank" >bell-to-bell policies.</a></p><p>I’m all for the ban. My 10-year-old doesn't have a cellphone or smartwatch (holding out for as long as I can!). Her Chicago Public Schools elementary school already has a locker policy for cellphones, which I obviously support. </p><p>But the issue is bigger than my kid and our school as social norms continue to shift with technology. I am happy to have a cap on some of the drama cellphones and TikTok can bring into the classroom. Some parents have pushed back against bans, citing the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/editorials/2025/02/24/cellphone-free-class-time-illinois-restriction-governor-pritzker-education" >need to reach</a> their children in an emergency. Um, that’s what the school main phone number is for. Worries about school shootings fuel some of the angst, but we have to trust school policies in case of an emergency. A part of me rejects that as a reason because technology affords us instant gratification, and parents want to exercise that right. They, too, are texting students in school about nonemergencies.</p><p>Admittedly, research around cellphone bans is a mixed bag. A <a class="Link" href="https://humsci.stanford.edu/feature/national-study-school-cellphone-bans-shows-benefits-are-not-immediate" target="_blank" >report earlier this year</a> from the National Bureau of Economic Research found over a three-year period, cellphone usage among middle and high school students decreased during the day. But there was no major impact on test scores, attendance or attention in class. The positives were improved disciplinary issues and higher student well-being. More research clearly needs to be conducted. But the policies aren’t causing harm.</p><p>I’m not naive. No-cellphone policies are not a panacea for social isolation or school improvement. As Illinois school districts finalize policies, this is an ideal time for parents to model imitable cellphone behavior, which brings me back to the aforementioned R&B concerts: the feeling of not being distracted and focusing on the songs. </p><p>Responsible device use can begin with parents and caregivers modeling good behavior. Picking up the cellphone to check for messages or a social media like is a habit like blinking. We don’t even think about it because it’s second nature. But we can be more intentional by putting away cellphones at meal times, turning off a cellphone when engaged in an activity or at an event and sleeping without the cellphone in the room. </p><p>Perhaps then our children will understand why keeping cellphones out of the classrooms isn’t punitive.</p><p><i>Natalie Y. Moore is a senior lecturer at Northwestern University. </i></p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-b70000" name="module-b70000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody">Send letters to <a class="Link" href="mailto:letters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" >letters@suntimes.com</a>. More about <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/submitting-opinion-and-letters" >how to submit here</a>.</div> </div><p></p>

entries.title: Are passive homes the answer to Chicago's severe weather?
entries.summary: <p>When storms pummeled northwest Indiana in August, the town of Beverly Shores was left without power for days. Some people were left in the dark for a week.</p><p>Violeta Burokas didn't know about the outage until she received an alert from her utility provider NIPSCO. Her home was fully powered thanks to energy stored from her rooftop solar panels.</p><p>“I didn't really even notice,” Burokas said. “I had friends coming over to charge things and spend the night so they could take a hot shower.”</p><p>So what set Burokas’ home apart from neighbors? Her passive house.</p><p>Passive homes are a type of building that drastically reduce energy use and carbon emissions, attracting growing interest in the United States, with Massachusetts, New York and Washington integrating passive home standards into their building codes. And passive building is starting to see lift off in Chicago, from single-family homes to one mixed-use development that will be the city's largest passive home project.</p><p>Burokas' property was built with triple-pane windows, an extra-thick layer of insulation and thicker walls. These kinds of elements mean the home's greenhouse gas emissions are close to net zero — and once she installs another handful of rooftop solar panels, she'll hit zero. </p><p>Her home’s extra energy is stored in batteries. When they're full, the excess power flows back into the grid.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" Miller hopes Burokas’ home being showcased in the American Solar Energy Society’s National Solar Tour, an open house for homes powered by solar, will help spread more awareness.</p><p>Burokas purchased the lot where her home sits when she was 22. After learning about passive homes from a friend, she tore down the old cottage on the site to build what she now considers her dream home.</p><p>Burokas has been able to weather the poor air quality caused by Canadian wildfires earlier this summer because of the building's air filtration system, in addition to severe storms like those last month.</p><p>“Even though me, personally, by myself, I'm not going to make a huge difference with climate change or anything like that, I didn't want to contribute to it,” she said.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div entries.title: Dear Abby: Opinions differ on multi-birthday gift exchange
entries.summary: <p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> I have a group of friends who get together once a month, usually for a casual dinner. Next month's gathering will be to celebrate three birthdays, one of which is mine. While planning this gathering (via text), I asked if we could skip exchanging presents and just enjoy our time together. The response from my friends was "No! We're doing presents." I know their intention is good; these are very generous friends. But I'm working only part time and have to pay for my health insurance out of pocket. They said I don't need to get them presents, but they will be getting me presents, so naturally I feel the pressure to reciprocate. While I'm not the most creative person, I could get away with making them something, but I'm also a bit put off. Shouldn't my wishes have been respected since it's my birthday? — <i>BIRTHDAY GIRL IN MASSACHUSETTS</i></p><p><b>DEAR BIRTHDAY GIRL:</b> Happy birthday! Your friends understand why you don't want to exchange gifts, and they want to give you something anyway. They aren't doing it to pressure you; they're doing it out of love. If giving them a handcrafted item would help you feel better, that's fine, but please don't feel disrespected by their generosity.</p><p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> My husband of two years and I are opposites when it comes to planning. He's spontaneous and acts on the spur of the moment. I'm the type who plans everything down to the last nanosecond (slight exaggeration).</p><p>Everything came to a head last Saturday when he suddenly decided to start a household project at 5 p.m. We were supposed to meet another couple for an evening out at 7. When he started the project, I reminded him of our date and asked him to let the other couple know that something had come up and we wouldn't make it. I thought he had taken care of it until they texted me at 7:15 wanting to know where we were. I texted back, "Been delayed, on my way." I dressed hurriedly, put on makeup in the car, broke all speed records and arrived there about 45 minutes late. I made excuses for him, knowing he has done this to them before. We were halfway through the meal when he showed up, wearing the same "work around the house" clothes from earlier. (I was surprised the hostess even seated him.) I was embarrassed, the other couple was understandably peeved, and I have had it with his inconsiderate behavior! Please advise. — <i>NOT OK IN OKLAHOMA</i></p><p><b>DEAR NOT OK:</b> If your husband doesn't know what a faux pas he committed by leaving the other couple hanging, tell him. His behavior was thoughtless and rude. Because you know he is forgetful, you should have kept asking him if he had made the call, or you could have done it yourself. I think your biggest mistake was trying to cover for him by fibbing. In the future, make sure you arrive promptly. Let him do his own explaining, make his own apologies and experience the fallout.</p><p><i>Dear Abby is written by Abigail Van Buren. For nearly four decades, Jeanne Phillips penned this column, which was founded in 1956 by her mother, Pauline Phillips. Contact Dear Abby at www.DearAbby.com or P.O. Box 270135, Kansas City, MO 64127.</i></p>

entries.title: How would you reimagine public transportation in Chicago? Here's what you told us
entries.summary: <p>We asked readers how they'd reimagine public transportation in Chicago. Here's what you told us, lightly edited for clarity.</p><p>Several people support reviving <a class="Link" href="https://www.transitchicago.com/planning/circle/" target="_blank" >the proposed CTA Circle Line</a>:</p><p>"Connect the spokes of the L with lines that circle the city instead of going downtown, where most people don't actually live or even hang out."<br><i>— John Fiebke</i></p><p>"Sometimes I want go from Pilsen to Logan Square and not drive or take the bus."<br><i>— Alex Valdivia</i></p><p>Other comments:</p><p>"Separate roads for bikers and pedestrians every few blocks, or mix with the one-ways."<br><i>— Aaron Robert Mayerle</i></p><p>"Remove parking and use the space for more protected bike lanes covered with solar cells to protect the riders from the elements and generate some clean energy."<br><i>— Alejandra Camacho</i></p><p>"Bus rapid transit on Western, Ashland, DuSable Lake Shore Drive and other arterials, creating a network of dedicated bus lanes that connect with bike and pedestrian infrastructure."<br><i>— Timothy Shambrook</i></p><p>"Extend the Blue Line to Mannheim instead of widening the Ike. More security on all trains and platforms. ... Lengthen the distance between stops on some bus lines; we probably don’t need a stop on every block."<br><i>— Eric Forte</i></p><p>"Electrify and make Metra frequent throughout the day."<br><i>— Jovan Mitrevski</i></p><p>"Have boats travel down the canal in the morning, bringing in people from the west burbs, then out in the evening."<br><i>— Paul Lopez</i></p><p>"Subsidize personalized conveyance: all-weather e-bikes (capable of hauling groceries, etc.) for the physically able, supplemented by a networked on-demand taxi-shuttle service tailored to those who aren't."<br><i>— Whitley Tee</i></p><p>"Free public transportation for elementary and high school students. And public transportation on the water during the summer. It would be dope to get on some type of ferry at 57th and ride all the way Downtown or further north."<br><i>— Eddie Meeks III</i></p><p>"Close some streets to cars and limit them to just bus and bike lanes. Example: Michigan Avenue from Wacker to Lake Shore Drive: one bus line, bikes and people. No cars. Also: express bus lanes in more parts of the city. Let the buses function as trolleys and be granted passage through red lights. If they move faster than traffic and are on time, people will use them."<br><i>— Rich Bykowski</i></p><p>"Bus priority signals at every intersection."<br><i>— Collin Pearsall</i></p>
